lede: A train pulls out of a station, runs at line speed, then brakes for the next one. Draw its velocity against time and the whole story is one line. Two readings come off it: how steeply the line rises, and how much space sits underneath it.
can: Read an acceleration as the gradient of one section.
Find a distance as the area under the line.
Split that area into triangles, rectangles and trapezia.

text: Speed up, hold steady, slow down

md: On a velocity-time graph the height is how fast, not how far. Two readings come off it and they answer different questions: the gradient of a section is its acceleration, the area underneath it the distance covered. Split the shape at every joint and the journey comes apart into pieces you can already work out.

text: 1. Three readings, and they never swap

md:
**Height** is the velocity at that instant. **Gradient** is the acceleration. **Area** between the line and the time axis is the distance travelled.

A horizontal section is now a steady velocity, not a body at rest. That is the one habit a displacement/time graph teaches you that has to be unlearned here.

prompt: On a velocity/time graph, the area under the graph gives the ____ travelled.
explain: Metres per second multiplied by seconds gives metres, so an area on these axes is a length of road.

md:
Take the two ends of a section, subtract the velocities for the rise, subtract the times for the run, and divide. The units follow: metres per second, per second, written m/s².

A falling section has a negative gradient, and that is a deceleration. Where a question asks for the deceleration, give its size and say what it is.

md:
Dashed lines at every joint cut the shape into pieces you already know: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 24 = 240$ m, then $30 \times 24 = 720$ m, then $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 30 \times 24 = 360$ m, giving $1320$ m.

The whole shape here is also a trapezium, so $\tfrac{1}{2}(80 + 30) \times 24$ gives the same $1320$ m in one line.

title: Why an area is a distance
md: A thin strip under the graph is a velocity multiplied by a short time, which is a short length of road. Add every strip and you have the whole journey. That is why the units come out in metres and why a flat section still adds distance.

prompt: A body's velocity rises uniformly from 8 m/s to 20 m/s over 15 s. How far does it travel, in metres?
explain: A trapezium: half of $(8 + 20)$, times 15, which is $14 \times 15 = 210$ m. Taking $20 \times 15$ would count the empty triangle above the line.

alt: A table of the pieces an area splits into: a rectangle is velocity times time; a triangle is half base times height; a trapezium is half the sum of the first and last velocities times the time; and the answer should sit between the two rectangles.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 404 210' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='404' height='210'><rect x='2' y='2' width='400' height='206' rx='8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1' stroke-opacity='0.5'/><path d='M6 76H398M6 106H398M6 136H398M6 166H398M6 196H398M136 46V196' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='0.8' stroke-opacity='0.45'/><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><text x='12' y='35' font-size='13.5' font-weight='600'>Split the area at every joint</text><text x='12' y='65' font-size='12' font-weight='600'>Piece</text><text x='142' y='65' font-size='12' font-weight='600'>Its area</text><text x='12' y='95' font-size='13'>rectangle</text><text x='142' y='95' font-size='13'>velocity × time</text><text x='12' y='125' font-size='13'>triangle</text><text x='142' y='125' font-size='13'>½ × base × height</text><text x='12' y='155' font-size='13'>trapezium</text><text x='142' y='155' font-size='13'>½ (first velocity + last) × time</text><text x='12' y='185' font-size='13'>a check</text><text x='142' y='185' font-size='13'>it sits between the two rectangles</text></g></svg>
caption: Three pieces, and one check worth ten seconds.

md:
A flat section gives a rectangle, a section starting or ending at rest gives a triangle, and any other sloping section gives a trapezium.

The check in the last row catches almost every slip: a stage from 9 m/s to 3 m/s over 30 s must cover more than $3 \times 30 = 90$ m and less than $9 \times 30 = 270$ m.

prompt: A stage falls from 9 m/s to 3 m/s over 30 s. Which answer is possible?
explain: It has to lie between 90 m and 270 m. The 360 m comes from leaving the one half out, and 45 m is far too small.

md:
It brakes from 18 m/s at 0.6 m/s² for 10 s, so $V = 18 - 0.6 \times 10 = 12$ m/s.
**First two stages:** $\tfrac{1}{2}(18 + 12) \times 10 = 150$ m, then $12 \times 25 = 300$ m, so 450 m.
**Still to run:** $600 - 450 = 150$ m.

prompt: You find the last braking stage takes 26 s, after 20 s of journey already gone. The question asks for the total time to the crossing. What do you write?
explain: $20 + 26 = 46$ s. The scheme gives a mark for finding the last stage's time and then adding on the seconds already elapsed, which is exactly this step.

md:
**Last stage:** a triangle of height 12, so $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 12 \times t = 150$ gives $t = 25$ s.
**Total time:** $10 + 25 + 25 = 60$ s.

title: Using Velocity Time Graphs to find Distance and Acceleration
why: The same two readings on one picture, at a slower pace. Watch how the area is split before anything is multiplied.

prompt: A body decelerates uniformly from 16 m/s to rest, covering 128 m. How many seconds does it take?
explain: The stage is a triangle: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 16 \times t = 128$, so $8t = 128$ and $t = 16$ s. Write the area, set it equal to the distance, solve.

md:
Start one clock when the first vehicle passes and call the time $T$. Write both distances as expressions in that same $T$: the bus covers $12T$, and the taxi covers $120 + 20(T - 20)$ once it is up to speed.

Level means equal distances from the same starting line, so set them equal and solve. The equation is linear, so no formula is needed.

prompt: In a catch-up question, what does 'draws level' tell you?
options: The two distances from the same starting line are equal
answer: The two distances from the same starting line are equal
explain: Level is about position, so the areas under the two graphs are equal. The velocities are usually quite different at that moment, which is why one is overtaking the other.

text: 7. Whose clock is the answer on?

alt: A table of the four steps of a catch-up: use one clock for both, started when the first vehicle passes; level means the two distances are equal; solving gives T on that shared clock; and the second vehicle has been going for T minus the head start.

md:
$T$ is measured from the first vehicle. If the question asks how long the second has been moving, take off its head start. If it asks for a total time to a finishing point, add back the seconds already gone before the last stage began.

Either way, read the question again before you write the number down.

prompt: A van passes a parked car and 6 s later the car starts. One clock, started when the van passed, gives $T = 33$ s when the car draws level. How many seconds has the car been moving?
explain: $33 - 6 = 27$ s. The car's own clock started 6 seconds late, so it has been going for 6 seconds less.

title: Sheet or memory?
md:
**On the Unit 2 sheet:** the quadratic formula, vector magnitude and angle, $v = u + at$, $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$, $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$ and $F = ma$. Nothing about graphs.
**Must be known:** gradient = acceleration; area = distance; the trapezium formula; and that one constant-acceleration formula covers one stage, never a whole journey.

prompt: Can you use $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$ across a whole journey that speeds up, holds steady, then brakes?
options: No, because the acceleration changes twice
Yes, as long as $u$ and $v$ are the first and last velocities
Yes, because the formula is on the sheet
answer: No, because the acceleration changes twice
explain: Every constant-acceleration formula assumes one steady acceleration. Across stages, the area under the graph is the only safe route.

The long version asks for a missing velocity, then a distance from the area, then a total time, eight to ten marks with follow-through. The first mark is the area of one named piece; the last is the quantity asked for, on the right clock. Stuck: dash a vertical line at each joint and work out the pieces you can.
